rate_limits: UNKNOWN - no published limit; one request per firm was made
licence: corporate website content; no open licence. Redistribution is not permitted for structured reuse.
historical_coverage: current vacancies only; pages are not archived by the employer
entity_identifiers: no identifier: vacancies are HTML fragments without stable ids
employer-specific requisition ids appear only inside the JS payloads we did not execute
timestamp_fields: generally absent from the HTML shell; posting dates live in client-rendered payloads
no reliable source_public_at can be obtained from the pages as fetched
known_limitations: An HTML careers page is a front door, not a job feed: 2 of 4 firm pages answered HTTP 200, one returned 403, one returned 404, and none of them contained vacancy records in the served HTML.
The Philips search-results page (200) is client-rendered: it contains no job entries in the HTML, so no records can be extracted without executing JavaScript, which this task does not do.

The Medtronic careers URL redirects to the corporate homepage; the page is a marketing page, so its many 'job'/'career' words are navigation text, not postings. Text counts are not evidence of hiring.
Without a publication timestamp in the HTML, first_observed_at would be the only clock - which cannot support any publication-relative analysis.
Page structure changes without notice and differs per firm per locale; a per-firm scraper is a maintenance burden with no cross-firm comparability.
Nothing here supports a technology-direction claim: vacancies are operational artefacts.
research_value: Establishes the fallback's real cost: for these five firms the only remaining hiring route is bespoke per-employer scraping of client-rendered pages, with no publication clock and no cross-firm comparability. That is the evidence needed to recommend against using hiring volume as a MedRadar signal for these firms at this stage.
